pathogen.value: Botulinum neurotoxin produced by Clostridium botulinum (mainly toxin types C and D in birds)

value: eating maggots or invertebrates that have fed on a decaying carcass (the carcass-maggot cycle)
eating decaying organic matter or contaminated feed directly
contaminated litter, boots or equipment carrying the bacteria onto a farm
leg weakness progressing to floppy paralysis of legs, wings, neck and eyelids
the classic limp, outstretched neck ('limberneck')
ruffled or quivering feathers that pull out easily
labored breathing
birds lying flat on their chest, eyes partly or fully closed, unable to lift their head
in broilers, sometimes diarrhea with excess urates

mortality.value: In chickens, death rates vary widely, from a few birds up to 40% of the flock; large numbers of wild waterfowl can die in bigger outbreaks

incubation_period.value: Ranges from about 2 hours to roughly 2 weeks after eating the toxin, depending on the dose

diagnosis.value: Based on typical signs plus lab detection of the toxin or the toxin-producing bacteria in blood, gut contents, feed or the environment; no visible lesions are found on post-mortem, which helps rule out other diseases

value: quickly removing and disposing of dead birds to break the carcass-maggot cycle
separating sick birds from healthy ones
replacing litter after an outbreak
controlling flies and rodents
cleaning and disinfecting with products effective against spore-forming bacteria
checking feed and water sources for contamination or dead animals
keeping poultry housed indoors rather than free-range, which lowers risk

treatment_overview.value: Some birds recover on their own or with supportive care; antitoxin can neutralize the toxin in the blood if available, and antibiotics have been used during outbreaks, but treatment can be limited or costly

when_to_call_vet.value: Call a vet promptly if birds show sudden leg weakness or a limp, outstretched neck, since this can progress quickly to paralysis and death.

summary.value: Botulism, also called limberneck, is caused not by an infection but by a powerful nerve toxin that chickens pick up from eating maggots or decaying matter containing the bacteria that make it. It causes progressive weakness and floppy paralysis starting in the legs, and while some birds recover with supportive care, prevention through quickly removing carcasses and good sanitation is the main defense.
